Rogue DHCP server on the network (192.168.1.66)
An unauthorised DHCP server 192.168.1.66 (08:00:27:3a:66:9e) sent 2 DHCP messages telling devices to use
When a device joins a network it shouts 'can someone give me an address?' (DHCP) and
trusts the first answer. A second server, 192.168.1.66, is answering too, and it tells devices to send
their traffic and name lookups through a device that is not your real router. That lets it watch or
redirect everything those devices do, while the addresses it hands out look completely normal.
Like a fake receptionist at the hotel entrance handing out room keys and directions that lead to their own
A rogue DHCP server at 08:00:27:3a:66:9e (an attacker's laptop or a tool like yersinia,
1. Find the port: look up 08:00:27:3a:66:9e in the switch MAC address table (
) or the router's client list, and disconnect it.
2. Enable DHCP snooping on the switch, trusting only the uplink to your real DHCP server.
3. On affected devices, renew the lease (
4. Treat traffic from affected devices as possibly intercepted: change important passwords.
Why we think it's an attack
It names itself (192.168.1.66) as the router instead of 192.168.1.1
It points clients' DNS at a local device (192.168.1.66) instead of 192.168.1.1
192.168.1.66 (08:00:27:3a:66:9e) hands out addresses in the same subnet as the real server
Why not “A second router is handing out addresses (192.168.1.66)”?
Nothing in the traffic pointed to a
misconfiguration. The stronger evidence: It names itself (192.168.1.66) as the router instead of
192.168.1.1; It points clients' DNS at a local device (192.168.1.66) instead of 192.168.1.1.
Someone is sending fake DNS answers for intranet-portal.example-bank.com, login.example-bank.com, pointing
↳ consequence of F1; fixing that should fix this too
DNS is the internet's phone book: it turns names into addresses. Here a device is
answering name lookups with fake addresses before (or instead of) the real server, so you may land on a
copy of a website built to steal passwords, or have your traffic secretly routed through the attacker.
Like someone swapping the numbers in your phone book so your calls to the bank reach a fraudster.
DNS spoofing from 192.168.1.66 (08:00:27:3a:66:9e), typically combined with ARP spoofing or
a rogue DHCP server (tools such as ettercap dns_spoof, bettercap, dnschef).
1. Find and disconnect 192.168.1.66 (08:00:27:3a:66:9e): look up its MAC in the switch MAC table or
3. Flush DNS caches on affected devices (
4. Check for ARP spoofing / rogue DHCP (
); enable DHCP snooping and Dynamic ARP
5. Use encrypted DNS (DoH/DoT) and HTTPS; treat credentials entered meanwhile as exposed.
Why we think it's an attack
The fake address 192.168.1.66 is the DNS server handed out by a second (rogue) DHCP server,
answering with its own address, not the router

Passwords are being sent unencrypted (HTTP Basic to 192.168.1.66:80)
3 logins to the HTTP Basic server 192.168.1.66:80 sent the username and password as readable text.
↳ consequence of F1; fixing that should fix this too
HTTP Basic is an old protocol that sends your login exactly as typed, without
encryption. Anyone who can capture traffic on the way (as this capture just did) could read and reuse the
password. Faultline only detected that a login happened; it never stores or shows the password itself.
Like writing your PIN on a postcard: every postman on the way can read it.
The HTTP Basic service on 192.168.1.66:80 accepts logins without TLS/SSH encryption.
1. Serve the site over HTTPS only (redirect port 80 to 443) so the login header is encrypted.
2. Prefer a proper login form or token over HTTP Basic, and enable HSTS.
3. Change the passwords that were used here: they must be considered exposed (1 device logged in:
4. Check the server's logs for logins from unknown addresses.
Why we think it's a misconfiguration
3 login messages for HTTP Basic to 192.168.1.66:80 travelled without encryption (3 sessions, 1
